William Kiffin
WIL-yum KIF-in
proper noun (figure)
English personal name. William (Germanic, "resolute protector"); Kiffin (also spelled Kiffen), an English surname. William Kiffin (1616-1701) was a leading Particular Baptist pastor and merchant of London.

Biblical Definition

William Kiffin (1616-1701) was the senior statesman of the 17th-century Particular Baptists — a London merchant of great wealth, a pastor for over sixty years, and a signatory of both the First (1644) and Second (1689) London Baptist Confessions. Orphaned young and apprenticed in the leather trade, Kiffin rose to become one of the wealthiest merchants in London, and he used his standing and resources to protect and advance the persecuted Baptist cause through the turbulent decades of the English Civil War, the Commonwealth, the Restoration, and the Glorious Revolution. He pastored the Devonshire Square congregation. His wealth and political connections repeatedly shielded Baptists from the worst of the persecution; he interceded with figures from Oliver Cromwell to Charles II to James II. Yet his life was marked by deep personal sorrow, including the execution of two grandsons in the aftermath of Monmouth's Rebellion (1685) and the famous incident in which James II tried to buy his loyalty by offering to make him an alderman, which Kiffin reluctantly accepted under royal pressure. He held firmly to a strict-communion Baptist position (that only the baptized — meaning believer-baptized — should be admitted to the Lord's Table), against the open-communion view of his friend John Bunyan, and the two engaged in a notable published exchange. Kiffin's long life spanned the entire founding era of the Particular Baptist movement, and his steady leadership, financial generosity, and confessional fidelity make him one of its indispensable fathers.

Webster 1828 Definition

Senior statesman of the 17th-century Particular Baptists (1616-1701); wealthy London merchant and pastor for over 60 years; signatory of both the 1644 and 1689 Confessions; protector of the persecuted Baptist cause; strict-communion advocate against Bunyan's open communion.

WILLIAM KIFFIN, proper noun. English Particular Baptist pastor and merchant (1616-1701).

Signatory of both the First (1644) and Second (1689) London Baptist Confessions; pastor of the Devonshire Square congregation.

One of the wealthiest merchants in London; used his standing to protect the persecuted Baptist cause across the Civil War, Commonwealth, Restoration, and Glorious Revolution.

Held a strict-communion position (only the believer-baptized admitted to the Table), debated in print against John Bunyan's open communion.

Suffered the execution of two grandsons after Monmouth's Rebellion (1685).

Key Scripture

1 Timothy 6:17-18 — "Charge them that are rich in this world, that they be not highminded, nor trust in uncertain riches, but in the living God... That they do good, that they be rich in good works, ready to distribute, willing to communicate."

Hebrews 10:34 — "For ye had compassion of me in my bonds, and took joyfully the spoiling of your goods, knowing in yourselves that ye have in heaven a better and an enduring substance."

Proverbs 13:22 — "A good man leaveth an inheritance to his children's children: and the wealth of the sinner is laid up for the just."

Acts 5:29 — "Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men."

Modern Corruption

William Kiffin is corrupted when his wealth is read as worldly compromise rather than stewarded for the persecuted church, when his strict-communion conviction is dismissed as narrow sectarianism, or when his political accommodations under royal pressure are judged without the context of brutal persecution.

expand to see more

Wealth-as-compromise misreading. A wealthy merchant-pastor can be read cynically, as though riches and gospel fidelity sit uneasily together. Kiffin's life answers the caricature: he used his wealth precisely as 1 Tim 6:17-18 commands — ready to distribute, willing to communicate — pouring his resources and his political standing into shielding the persecuted Baptist churches through decades when imprisonment, fines, and worse were the constant threat. His money bought protection for the saints, not luxury for himself. The Reformed reader honors a man who held great wealth with an open hand for the church's good.

Strict-communion-as-narrowness misreading. Kiffin's insistence that only the believer-baptized be admitted to the Lord's Table is often dismissed as needless sectarian narrowness, especially set against the warm open-communion of his friend Bunyan. The strict-communion position rests on a serious argument: that baptism is the divinely-appointed entry to the visible church and the Table, so that to admit the unbaptized is to invert the biblical order. Reformed Baptists have held both views across their history; the dictionary presents Kiffin's position as a serious confessional conviction, argued from the order of the ordinances, not as mere narrowness.
